newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Court overturns Manila Hotel sale to Malaysia firm.
newsitem.headline: Court overturns Manila Hotel sale to Malaysia firm.

text.p: The Philippine Supreme Court on Monday awarded the sale of the historic Manila Hotel to a Filipino company, throwing out the winning bid of Malaysian infrastructure development firm Renong Berhad.
The Supreme Court ordered the Government Service and Insurance System (GSIS), the owners of the hotel, to sell the property to the Manila Prince Hotel Corporation.
The decision ends a legal battle that began in October 1995 when Manila Prince, after losing its bid to buy 51 percent of the hotel, petitioned the Supreme Court.
It said the hotel was part of the national heritage and should not be sold to a foreign entity.
Facing Manila Bay, Manila Hotel is considered one of the great luxury heritage hotels in Asia and served as the U.S. military headquarters during World War Two.
Renong, along with ITT Sheraton, a unit of the U.S. ITT Corp, had bid 673.20 million pesos ($25.6 million), or 44 pesos per share, for the 51 percent stake.
Prince's losing bid was 636.174 million pesos, or 41.58 pesos per share, but it later said it was willing to match Renong's bid.
A 15-judge panel of the Supreme Court said in an 11-4 decision that the sale should be granted to Manila Prince to uphold a "Filipino First Policy" in the constitution.

"Since the Filipino First Policy provision of the Constitution bestows preference on qualified Filipinos, the mere tending of the highest bid is not an assurance that the highest bidder will be declared the winning bidder," the court said.

"Where a foreign firm submits the highest bid in a public bidding concerning the grant of rights, privileges and concessions covering the national economy and patrimony, thereby exceeding the bid of a Filipino, there is no question that the Filipino will have to be allowed to match the bid of the foreign entity. And if the Filipino matches the bid of a foreign firm, the award should go to the Filipino."
Businessman Emilio Yap, who owns Manila Prince and is also chairman of one of the largest circulated newspapers in the country, the Manila Bulletin, could not be reached for comment.
Officials of Renong were also unavailable.

The decision to set aside the sale of a government asset after the bidding process has been completed is the latest in a series of cases that have raised fears that foreign businesses might be discouraged from investing in the country.

Last week, the Philippine Court of Appeals temporarily halted the privatisation of the Manila Waterworks System in response to a petition which questioned the government's authority to go ahead with the deal. The government had already announced the winners of the two concessions offered.
Earlier this year, President Fidel Ramos ordered rebidding in the privatisation of a container terminal at Subic Port near Manila.

In 1995, a contract won by Hong Kong's Consolidated Electric Power Asia, then a unit of Hopewell Holdings, to build a power station was set aside after it was found the company would use banned technology.
The frequent upsetting of contracts on account of intervention by the courts or the government has been severely criticised by newspaper columnists, analysts and businessmen.

"This tells foreign investors that the Philippines is not exactly the kind of lake the fish can swim in. It sends a very very bad signal because it comes from the highest court of the land," political analyst Teodoro Benigno said.

The Supreme Court judgment said: "This court does not discount the apprehension that this (Filipino First) policy may discourage foreign investors ... These are given factors which investors must consider when venturing into business in a foreign jurisdiction."
